lesson_title: One Company, Four Statements, Every Mark
hook_text: A pizzeria slice the books value at 473 cents sells between cousins for 540. Who is wrong?
clip_script: A family pizzeria became a company — seven hundred and thirty thousand slices of ownership. The books are honest: everything the pizzeria owns, minus everything it owes, comes to about four hundred and seventy-three cents a slice. Yet cousins pay five hundred and forty cents. Sixty-seven cents above the honest number. Are they fools? No — they are buying what the books are forbidden to record: the corner location, the customers who queue every evening, next year's pizzas. The books look backward; the price looks forward. Now flip the question every analysis task loves. Each slice EARNED seventy cents this year — that is earnings per share. Each slice was PAID forty-five cents — that is the dividend. The missing twenty-five cents did not vanish; it stayed inside, making every slice quietly heavier. And the family money itself? It earned sixteen comma nine cents per rand while a bank deposit pays about eight — nearly nine cents of reward for risk. Meanwhile the pizzeria borrows at twelve and puts the money to work earning twenty comma four. Every borrowed rand earns more than it eats. That is the whole of company analysis: two numbers, same units, one comparison, one judgement. Books against market. Earned against paid. Business against bank. Loan cost against return. Master those four comparisons and the analysis question becomes the friendliest marks you will meet.
visual_style: A pizza slice split into layered coins — book value stacking to 473, a golden 67-cent halo appearing above it; then a balance beam weighing 70 earned against 45 paid, with 25 cents sliding back into the slice.
pacing: Curious open on the price gap, steady reveal of the halo, brisk drumbeat through the four comparisons.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision session and walk into your final exams with all four comparisons in your pocket.
